name: Ryan Detrick, CMT
zh_summary: @RyanDetrick says his contrarian call that the 9.1% Feb/March correction would be the year's largest pullback is holding, despite bulls cutting targets in July. This may be the earliest max peak to trough correction in a midterm year since 1958.
en_summary: @RyanDetrick says his contrarian call that the 9.1% Feb/March correction would be the year's largest pullback is holding, despite bulls cutting targets in July. This may be the earliest max peak to trough correction in a midterm year since 1958.
text:
One of our more contrarian calls was the 9.1% mild correction we saw in Feb/March would be the largest pullback of the year. We started to say that back in May and this wasn't a popular call. 

In July, many bulls were cutting their targets and calling for a bear market in Q3. The reasoning was midterm years tend to see the largest corrections.

This could now be the earliest max peak-to-trough correction in a midterm year since 1958.

text:
A TON OF THINGS HAPPENED IN THE STOCK MARKET TODAY.

Here's a full recap:

1. Q3 2026 earnings season got underway with reports from JPMorgan $JPM, Goldman Sachs $GS, Citigroup $C, and Wells Fargo $WFC, delivering a mixed but generally resilient picture for the banking sector. Goldman Sachs led the group with a standout quarter, posting its second-best revenue quarter ever as equities trading surged 72%, while Citigroup reported its strongest third quarter in a decade, driven by strength in services, wealth management, and equities. JPMorgan delivered a rare earnings miss despite raising its 2026 net interest income outlook, and Wells Fargo beat on earnings but missed on revenue. Across the sector, banks continued to describe the U.S. consumer as resilient, highlighted ongoing AI-driven corporate investment, raised or maintained optimistic net interest income expectations, and pointed to strong equity trading activity, while cautioning that sticky inflation, higher-for-longer interest rates, elevated valuations, and geopolitical risks remain key challenges heading into 2027.

2. Bank of America said 10-year U.S. Treasury yields may need to approach 6% before investors meaningfully rotate out of stocks and into bonds, according to its latest Global Fund Manager Survey. The survey found 76% of respondents expect the Fed to leave rates unchanged in October, while technology allocations climbed to their highest level since August 2020 and long semiconductors remained the market’s

name: Nick Timiraos
zh_summary: @NickTimiraos lays out the Lisa Cook chronology: Supreme Court ruled for Cook June 29; Trump vowed to restart removal July 2; WH letters Aug 5; FOMC voted unanimously to raise rates Sept 16; Oct 7 Trump created a three person committee and set a Nov 5 hearing; Cook's lawyer responded Oct 13.
en_summary: @NickTimiraos lays out the Lisa Cook chronology: Supreme Court ruled for Cook June 29; Trump vowed to restart removal July 2; WH letters Aug 5; FOMC voted unanimously to raise rates Sept 16; Oct 7 Trump created a three person committee and set a Nov 5 hearing; Cook's lawyer responded Oct 13.
text:
With the latest letter, we now have the following chronology:

June 29: Supreme Court rules in Cook's favor
July 2: Trump tells CNBC he'll restart efforts to remove Cook by adhering to "perfect process and perfect procedure"
Aug 5: WH (Scavino) asks Cook to explain the allegations made against her in a letter, and for the response to be made within 3 week
Aug 26: Cook's attorneys respond
Sept 16: FOMC unanimous vote to raise rates
Sept 30: Scavino writes about a potential hearing, date proposed for Oct. 14
Oct 5: Cook's attorney (Lowell) responds, seeking more information about a hearing and saying Oct. 14 won't work
Oct 7: Trump signs memo creating three-person committee to investigate Cook, sets Nov. 5 in-person hearing
Oct 8: WH (Scharf) sends letter to Cook/Lowell
Oct 9: Trump memo is made public
Oct 13: Lowell responds

name: Cullen Roche
zh_summary: @cullenroche: long Treasuries are the only asset paying real income that tends to rally in a crash, but mainly in deflationary or growth scares like 2008, and they bleed in real terms most of the time. OTM puts are true crash insurance but cost money to hold. Safe income in long duration assets is a myth; dividend paying consumer staples come closest, while distribution yield and buffered income funds are mostly marketing.
en_summary: @cullenroche: long Treasuries are the only asset paying real income that tends to rally in a crash, but mainly in deflationary or growth scares like 2008, and they bleed in real terms most of the time. OTM puts are true crash insurance but cost money to hold. Safe income in long duration assets is a myth; dividend paying consumer staples come closest, while distribution yield and buffered income funds are mostly marketing.
text:
Tough question. Income with crash hedging but not stocks, credit or MF? Long Treasuries are the only thing that pays you real income and tends to rally in a crash. The catch is they only work in a deflationary or growth scare like 2008. That's the plain vanilla tail hedge with income, but long bonds are terrible long duration assets to hold because they bleed in real terms most of the time. 

OTM puts are true crash insurance in any environment, but they cost you money to wait. 

Frankly, I think the idea of "safe" income in a long duration asset is a bit like turning water into wine. Lots of products claim to provide it, but there are huge trade-offs in the long run so I'd personally treat income as safe income and long duration hedgers as something different. Dividend paying consumer staples might be as close as you can get to the holy grail of equity+income (but even those are paying out of tax efficient capital). These popular distribution yield funds and all the income buffered stuff are good marketing materials, but mostly counterproductive compared to something like home grown dividend strategies....
